title: U.S. House · North Carolina's 11th District
area: Western North Carolina, including Asheville and Buncombe County and all or part of Avery, Cherokee, Clay, Graham, Haywood, Henderson, Jackson, Macon, Madison, McDowell, Mitchell, Polk, Rutherford, Swain, Transylvania, and Yancey counties.

context.text: Incumbent Chuck Edwards won the March 3, 2026 Republican primary, but ended his re-election campaign on August 5, 2026, after the House Ethics Committee released a report finding he had "engaged in persistent unprofessional and inappropriate conduct" toward two female staffers and recommending he be censured. The 11th District Republican Party executive committee selected North Carolina House member Jennifer Balkcom on August 10, 2026 to replace Edwards as the Republican nominee on the November ballot. Jamie Ager won a five-way Democratic primary.

The Ethics Committee's report, based on a 25-page investigation, described Edwards giving two young staffers "lavish" gifts including jewelry, designer purses, and a KitchenAid mixer, inviting them on "intimate dinners and vacations," and sending personal notes; it said both staffers eventually left his office. Edwards's attorneys responded that the findings did not establish sexual harassment under House rules and that he "sincerely regrets that his behavior created discomfort," while his campaign said he "looks forward to having his name cleared."
On September 1, 2026, the full House voted 413-2 to agree to H. Res. 1498, "In the matter of allegations relating to Representative Chuck Edwards," censuring him.
Edwards remains a sitting member of Congress representing the 11th District through the end of his term but is not on the November 3, 2026 general election ballot.

candidates.name: Jamie Ager

summary.text: Jamie Ager is the Democratic nominee for North Carolina's 11th Congressional District. A Fairview farmer and co-founder of the meat company Hickory Nut Gap, he won the March 3 Democratic primary; according to his campaign website, he is running on Hurricane Helene recovery, affordability for working families, and preserving the environment and local culture.

background.text: Born in Fairview, North Carolina, and, according to his campaign website, raised on his family's Hickory Nut Gap Farm, where he describes himself as a fourth-generation farmer.

Graduated from A.C. Reynolds High School and earned degrees from Warren Wilson College in environmental studies (with a concentration in sustainable agriculture) and history, where he met his wife, Amy.
According to his campaign website, he took part in an agriculture leadership development program through NC State from 2004 to 2006.
Co-founded Hickory Nut Gap, which he describes as a sustainable meat company; his campaign website says it supports 25 employees and works with dozens of farmers across the region.
Has been affiliated with the Buncombe County Farm Bureau and the Carolina Farm Stewardship Association.
His campaign website says his grandfather, Jamie Clarke, served in the U.S. Congress and the state legislature, and that his father, John, held the state House seat now held by his brother, Eric.

According to his campaign website, his family lost power and water for weeks after Hurricane Helene; WSOC-TV reported that the farm was heavily affected by the storm and that it lost a beef contract with local schools after federal agriculture cuts.
Won the March 3, 2026 Democratic primary for the 11th District, defeating four other candidates with 64.7% of the vote. According to his campaign website, he is the father of three sons.

priorities.text: Points to rising costs, Medicaid cuts, and increasingly severe weather as issues affecting his neighbors and his farm business.
priorities.quote: Rising costs hurt our businesses and our families. Medicaid insures my neighbors and my friends and now it's being ripped away. And the weather that batters us is only getting worse.

priorities.text: Frames his campaign as opposing policies he says favor wealthy interests over working Americans.
priorities.quote: Helping the rich get richer on the backs of hardworking Americans isn't working. In my humble opinion, it doesn't have to be this way.

positions.summary: His campaign platform says he will push for a public option and support Medicaid and Medicare.
positions.quote: I’ll push for a public option so everyone has access to quality affordable health care.

positions.summary: His campaign platform says he will push to reform the tax code so those at the top pay their fair share.
positions.quote: I’ll push both parties to reform the tax code so the folks at the top pay their fair share.

positions.summary: His campaign platform says he will back more investment in law enforcement pay and training.
positions.quote: We must invest in better pay and training for our law enforcement officers, as well as programs that help tackle the root causes of crime.

statements.quote: We need more housing for owners and renters.
I’ll push to expand grants and the child tax credit for young families.
I support reforms that treat people with dignity and give businesses the workforce they need to grow, all while keeping every community safe.

candidates.researchNotes: Additional positions and statements added from his campaign platform page. He has not completed a Ballotpedia Candidate Connection survey. His platform page does not address abortion, guns, climate, tariffs, or Israel.

candidates.name: Jennifer Balkcom
candidates.currentRole: Member, North Carolina House of Representatives, District 117 (since 2023)
candidates.ballotNote: Selected by the North Carolina Republican Party to replace Chuck Edwards on the general-election ballot after he ended his re-election campaign following an Ethics Committee censure recommendation. Balkcom had won her own re-election primary for her state House seat but will not appear on that ballot in November.

summary.text: Jennifer Balkcom is the Republican nominee for North Carolina's 11th Congressional District. A Henderson County mortgage loan officer and small business owner, she has represented District 117 in the North Carolina House since 2023. She was selected by the district Republican Executive Committee on August 10, 2026, to replace Rep. Chuck Edwards on the ballot, and says she is running on affordability, community safety, support for farmers and Hurricane Helene recovery.

background.text: Born in Henderson County, North Carolina; according to her campaign website, she is an eighth-generation Western North Carolinian who grew up on her family's apple farm.
Graduated from East Henderson High School and earned an associate degree from Blue Ridge Community College (business administration, banking and finance, per her campaign website) in 2016.

According to her campaign website, she began a career in banking and finance in 1998 and is now a mortgage loan officer and small business owner; she has served as treasurer of the Mortgage Bankers Association of Western North Carolina.

Has served as vice president of the Hendersonville Women's Club and the Hendersonville Lions Club, and on the boards of the Henderson County Education Foundation, the AdventHealth Foundation and the Henderson County Planning Board.

Elected to the North Carolina House of Representatives in 2022, representing District 117; assigned to the Agriculture, Banking, House Finance, Local Government (Land Use, Planning and Development), and State Government committees in the 2023-2024 session.

WLOS reported that in the General Assembly she chairs the Appropriations Committee on Agriculture, Natural and Economic Resources and the Insurance Committee, and is vice chair of the Appropriations Committee and the House Select Committee on Helene Recovery.
Became the Republican nominee on August 10, 2026, when the district's Republican Executive Committee unanimously chose her from six candidates after Rep. Chuck Edwards withdrew from the race.
According to her campaign website, she lives in Hendersonville with her family.

priorities.text: Points to sponsoring House Bill 805, the Prevent Sexual Exploitation of Women and Minors Act, and other criminal justice measures as a legislative priority.
priorities.quote: This session, Jennifer expanded her work on protecting women and children with House Bill 805, the Prevent Sexual Exploitation of Women and Minors Act, a major piece of legislation that strengthens protections against exploitation and abuse and is now state law.

priorities.text: Says protecting North Carolina farmland from foreign ownership and securing disaster relief for farmers are among her legislative priorities, drawing on growing up on a family farm in Henderson County.
priorities.quote: Jennifer's key initiatives in NC agriculture include legislation to provide disaster relief for farmers affected by natural disasters... and efforts to prevent discrimination in financing against agricultural producers. Additionally, she has introduced the NC Farmland and Military Protection Act to safeguard U.S. farmland from foreign ownership.

priorities.text: In a campaign ad, said she led an effort in the state legislature to prevent foreign ownership of North Carolina farmland.
priorities.quote: Protecting family farms is personal to me. That's why I led the effort in Raleigh to stop China and other enemies from owning or buying our farmland.

positions.summary: As a state representative she was lead sponsor of House Bill 574, the Fairness in Women's Sports Act, which bars transgender athletes from women's school sports; it became law in 2023 over the governor's veto.
positions.quote: Girls should not have to worry about having to compete against biological males in sports, and this legislation will protect female athletes from such unfair and unsafe competition.

record.text: Sponsored North Carolina House Bill 805 (Prevent Sexual Exploitation of Women and Minors Act), which was signed into state law.
Sponsored the North Carolina Farmland and Military Protection Act, to restrict foreign ownership of North Carolina farmland.
Elected to the North Carolina House of Representatives in 2022, representing District 117; served on the Agriculture, Banking, House Finance, Local Government, and State Government committees.

candidates.name: Travis Groo

summary.text: Travis Groo is the Libertarian candidate for North Carolina's 11th Congressional District. He works in transportation and has run as a Libertarian for the North Carolina legislature several times. In his Ballotpedia survey he lists balancing the budget, eliminating the income tax and abolishing Certificate of Need laws as his key messages.

background.text: Earned a bachelor's degree from the University of West Florida in 2000; lists transportation as his profession.

Ran as the Libertarian candidate for North Carolina House District 11 in 2018 and for North Carolina Senate District 17 in 2020, and was listed as a withdrawn Libertarian candidate for North Carolina House District 41 in 2022.
Was the Libertarian candidate for North Carolina House District 36 in 2024, receiving 1,521 votes out of 52,514 cast.
Is on the November 3, 2026 ballot for the 11th Congressional District after the Libertarian primary was canceled.

priorities.text: Lists balancing the federal budget, eliminating the federal income tax, and abolishing Certificate of Need laws as his three key campaign messages.
priorities.quote: Balance the budget. Get rid of the income tax. Abolish Certificate of Need (CON) laws.

priorities.text: Says property rights are the public policy area he is most passionate about.

statements.quote: If Americans want immigrants to enter through legal channels, we need to make those channels fair, reasonable, and accessible.
statements.context: In answers to a WLOS (News 13) candidate questionnaire, Oct. 15, 2026

statements.quote: Get rid of the income tax.
statements.context: In his 2026 Ballotpedia Candidate Connection survey, on the federal income tax

candidates.researchNotes: Positions come from his 2026 Ballotpedia Candidate Connection survey and WLOS candidate questionnaire. No campaign website was found (Ballotpedia lists only social media accounts).

researchNotes: Chuck Edwards is the sitting incumbent but is not a general-election candidate; his ethics case is described in context, sourced to Blue Ridge Public Radio's reporting on the House Ethics Committee report, rather than being treated as an unproven allegation. The August 5 withdrawal date, the August 10 selection of Jennifer Balkcom, and the September 1 House censure vote (413-2, Roll Call 292) were independently confirmed against The Epoch Times and the official Clerk of the House roll-call record, since the original BPR source predated those events. Travis Groo (Libertarian) has a minimal public record beyond his brief candidate survey answers. Biography detail for Travis Groo is limited to his Ballotpedia profile; no campaign website or news profile with personal background was found.
